Food Delivery Orders and Customer Behavior Analysis

Mayank Saini

2026-09-16

1. Introduction

Food delivery services have become an important part of the modern food and restaurant industry. Customers can order food from different restaurants through online delivery platforms, making it possible to analyze ordering patterns, food costs, delivery performance and customer satisfaction.

This project analyzes food delivery order data using R. The analysis focuses on order costs, delivery charges, preparation time, delivery time, customer ratings, cuisines, restaurants and order status.

Statistical analysis and data visualization techniques are used to identify patterns and relationships in the food delivery data.

2. Objectives

The main objectives of this project are:

  • To import and understand the food delivery dataset.
  • To examine the structure and characteristics of the data.
  • To identify missing and duplicate values.
  • To clean and preprocess the dataset.
  • To analyze food and delivery costs.
  • To analyze preparation and delivery times.
  • To compare different cuisine types.
  • To analyze restaurant performance.
  • To study customer ratings.
  • To analyze order status.
  • To examine relationships between numerical variables.
  • To create meaningful graphs and visualizations.
  • To identify important findings and provide recommendations.

3. Data Importing

Explanation of the R Code

The read.csv() function is used to import the food delivery CSV file into R. The imported dataset is stored in an object called food_data.

# Load required package
library(ggplot2)

# Import the CSV dataset
food_data <- read.csv("food_delivery_orders.csv")

5. Data Preprocessing and Cleaning

Data cleaning is an important step before statistical analysis. It helps ensure that the results are based on valid and consistent observations.

5.1 Check Missing Values

missing_values <- colSums(is.na(food_data))

missing_values
##            Order_ID         Customer_ID     Restaurant_Name        Cuisine_Type 
##                   0                   0                   0                   0 
##           Food_Cost        Delivery_Fee    Total_Order_Cost       Prep_Time_Min 
##                   0                   0                   0                   0 
##   Delivery_Time_Min Total_Delivery_Time        Order_Rating        Order_Status 
##                   0                   0                   0                   0

Interpretation

The number of missing values is displayed for every variable. Variables with missing values can affect statistical calculations and therefore need to be considered during preprocessing.

5.2 Check Duplicate Records

duplicate_count <- sum(duplicated(food_data))

cat("Number of duplicate records:", duplicate_count)
## Number of duplicate records: 0

Interpretation

Duplicate records can result in the same order being counted more than once. The result above shows whether duplicate observations are present.

5.3 Check Data Types

sapply(food_data, class)

6. Creating a Clean Dataset

food_clean <- food_data

# Remove duplicate records
food_clean <- food_clean[!duplicated(food_clean), ]

# Remove rows with missing important numerical values
food_clean <- food_clean[
  !is.na(food_clean$Food_Cost) &
  !is.na(food_clean$Delivery_Fee) &
  !is.na(food_clean$Total_Order_Cost) &
  !is.na(food_clean$Prep_Time_Min) &
  !is.na(food_clean$Delivery_Time_Min) &
  !is.na(food_clean$Order_Rating),
]

# Keep positive cost and time values
food_clean <- food_clean[
  food_clean$Food_Cost >= 0 &
  food_clean$Delivery_Fee >= 0 &
  food_clean$Total_Order_Cost >= 0 &
  food_clean$Prep_Time_Min >= 0 &
  food_clean$Delivery_Time_Min >= 0,
]

cat("Original number of records:", nrow(food_data), "\n")
## Original number of records: 100
cat("Records after cleaning:", nrow(food_clean), "\n")
## Records after cleaning: 100
cat("Records removed:", nrow(food_data) - nrow(food_clean))
## Records removed: 0

Explanation

The dataset is copied into food_clean. Duplicate observations are removed, followed by observations with missing important numerical values.

Negative values for costs and delivery times are also excluded because they are not meaningful for this analysis.

Interpretation

The cleaned dataset contains valid observations that can be used for the remaining statistical analysis.

  Standard_Deviation = sd(food_clean$Food_Cost)
)

8. Order Status Analysis

status_count <- table(food_clean$Order_Status)

status_count
## 
## Delivered 
##       100

Order Status Visualization

status_data <- as.data.frame(status_count)

names(status_data) <- c("Order_Status", "Number_of_Orders")

ggplot(
  status_data,
  aes(x = Order_Status, y = Number_of_Orders)
) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Food Delivery Order Status",
    x = "Order Status",
    y = "Number of Orders"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

Interpretation

The bar chart shows the number of orders belonging to each order status. This helps identify the proportion of orders that were successfully delivered and those that may have experienced another status.

9. Cuisine Type Analysis

cuisine_count <- table(food_clean$Cuisine_Type)

cuisine_count
## 
##      American       Chinese        Indian       Italian      Japanese 
##            13            13            13            13            12 
## Mediterranean       Mexican          Thai 
##            12            12            12

Cuisine Visualization

cuisine_data <- as.data.frame(cuisine_count)

names(cuisine_data) <- c("Cuisine_Type", "Number_of_Orders")

ggplot(
  cuisine_data,
  aes(
    x = reorder(Cuisine_Type, Number_of_Orders),
    y = Number_of_Orders
  )
) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Number of Orders by Cuisine Type",
    x = "Cuisine Type",
    y = "Number of Orders"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

Interpretation

The graph compares the popularity of different cuisine types based on the number of orders. Cuisine types with larger bars received more orders in the dataset.

18. Delivery Time and Customer Rating

ggplot(
  food_clean,
  aes(
    x = Delivery_Time_Min,
    y = Order_Rating
  )
) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm",
    se = FALSE
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Relationship Between Delivery Time and Customer Rating",
    x = "Delivery Time (Minutes)",
    y = "Customer Rating"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
## `geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'

Interpretation

The scatter plot examines whether delivery time is associated with customer ratings. The trend line provides a simple visual indication of the direction of the relationship.

A relationship in the graph should not automatically be interpreted as causation.

20. Correlation Analysis

Correlation measures the strength and direction of a linear relationship between numerical variables.

correlation_data <- food_clean[
  ,
  c(
    "Food_Cost",
    "Delivery_Fee",
    "Total_Order_Cost",
    "Prep_Time_Min",
    "Delivery_Time_Min",
    "Order_Rating"
  )
]

correlation_matrix <- cor(
  correlation_data,
  use = "complete.obs"
)

round(correlation_matrix, 3)
##                   Food_Cost Delivery_Fee Total_Order_Cost Prep_Time_Min
## Food_Cost             1.000        0.949            1.000         0.895
## Delivery_Fee          0.949        1.000            0.956         0.868
## Total_Order_Cost      1.000        0.956            1.000         0.896
## Prep_Time_Min         0.895        0.868            0.896         1.000
## Delivery_Time_Min     0.260        0.256            0.260         0.514
## Order_Rating          0.120        0.095            0.118        -0.177
##                   Delivery_Time_Min Order_Rating
## Food_Cost                     0.260        0.120
## Delivery_Fee                  0.256        0.095
## Total_Order_Cost              0.260        0.118
## Prep_Time_Min                 0.514       -0.177
## Delivery_Time_Min             1.000       -0.841
## Order_Rating                 -0.841        1.000

Explanation

The cor() function calculates correlation coefficients.

Correlation values range from -1 to +1:

  • A value close to +1 indicates a strong positive relationship.
  • A value close to -1 indicates a strong negative relationship.
  • A value close to 0 indicates a weak linear relationship.

Interpretation

The correlation matrix helps identify relationships among food cost, delivery fee, total order cost, preparation time, delivery time and customer ratings.

  Total_Orders = nrow(food_clean),

  Unique_Restaurants = length(unique(food_clean$Restaurant_Name)),
  Unique_Cuisines = length(unique(food_clean$Cuisine_Type)),
  Average_Food_Cost = mean(food_clean$Food_Cost),
  Average_Delivery_Fee = mean(food_clean$Delivery_Fee),
  Average_Order_Cost = mean(food_clean$Total_Order_Cost),
  Average_Delivery_Time = mean(food_clean$Delivery_Time_Min),
  Average_Rating = mean(food_clean$Order_Rating)
)

23. Findings

Based on the statistical analysis and visualizations, the following findings were identified:

  • The dataset contains detailed information about food delivery orders.
  • Food costs and total order costs vary across different orders.
  • Different cuisine types have different levels of popularity.
  • Restaurant order counts vary, indicating differences in customer demand.
  • Delivery times vary among orders.
  • Food preparation time contributes to the overall delivery process.
  • Customer ratings provide an indication of customer satisfaction.
  • The relationship between delivery time and customer rating can be examined using correlation and scatter-plot analysis.
  • Food cost has an important relationship with total order cost.
  • The analysis demonstrates how statistical methods and visualization can be used to understand food delivery operations and customer behavior.

24. Business Recommendations

Based on the analysis, the following recommendations can be considered:

  • Restaurants should monitor preparation times to improve delivery efficiency.
  • Delivery services should identify orders with unusually long delivery times.
  • Restaurants can study popular cuisine categories to understand customer demand.
  • Customer ratings can be used to identify areas requiring service improvement.
  • Restaurants can analyze average order values to understand customer spending behavior.
  • Delivery charges should be monitored to maintain a balance between customer satisfaction and operational costs.

25. Conclusion

This project analyzed food delivery order data using R.

The analysis included data importing, preprocessing, data cleaning, descriptive statistics, order analysis, cuisine analysis, restaurant analysis, cost analysis, delivery-time analysis, customer rating analysis, customer analysis and correlation analysis.

Various graphs were created to visualize important patterns and relationships within the dataset. Statistical measures were used to summarize the data and support the interpretation of results.

Overall, the project demonstrates how R can be used for practical data analysis and visualization in the food delivery industry. The results can help understand customer behavior, restaurant demand, order costs and delivery performance.

26. Explanation of R Functions Used

R Function Purpose
read.csv() Imports CSV data
head() Displays first records
nrow() Counts rows
ncol() Counts columns
names() Displays column names
str() Shows dataset structure
summary() Provides summary statistics
is.na() Identifies missing values
duplicated() Identifies duplicate records
unique() Finds unique values
table() Creates frequency tables
mean() Calculates average
median() Calculates median
min() Finds minimum
max() Finds maximum
sd() Calculates standard deviation
aggregate() Calculates grouped statistics
cor() Calculates correlation
ggplot() Creates visualizations
geom_col() Creates bar charts
geom_histogram() Creates histograms
geom_point() Creates scatter plots
geom_smooth() Adds a trend line
theme_minimal() Applies a clean graph theme
